abstracts.abstract: This paper presents Compositional Interface Theory (CIT), a fundamentally new mathematical framework for modeling and verifying cyber-physical systems that tightly integrate discrete control logic with physical dynamics. Existing approaches to hybrid systems modeling treat discrete and continuous dynamics as separate concerns, leading to state-space explosion and poor scalability in verification. CIT proposes that CPS can be decomposed into components with formally defined interfaces capturing energy, information, and temporal coupling, enabling a paradigm shift from monolithic analysis to compositional reasoning. The framework introduces interface theories rooted in Assume-Guarantee contracts extended with physical semantics, where each component's behavior is characterized by a set of admissible trajectories and a compatibility relation. We prove that the composition of components satisfying their interface contracts yields a system that preserves safety properties (safety composition theorem). Furthermore, we show that verification reduces to checking contract satisfaction at component boundaries rather than exploring the full state space. The approach is validated on a benchmark suite of automotive and aerospace CPS case studies, demonstrating exponential reduction in verification time compared to conventional model checking while maintaining soundness. CIT establishes a new theoretical foundation for CPS development that fundamentally reconceives the relationship between abstraction and verification in embedded systems.

Real-time embedded systems increasingly operate under multi-mode execution requirements, yet existing schedulability analysis techniques fail to adequately address mode transitions with guaranteed quality-of-service. This paper presents an enhanced response-time analysis framework for multi-mode real-time tasks under fixed-priority scheduling, substantially advancing the state of the art in control systems scheduling theory. We introduce Mode-Aware Response-Time Analysis (MARTA), which extends classical worst-case response-time computation by explicitly modeling the temporal cost and control performance impact of mode transitions. The key innovation lies in a novel analytical bound on transition-induced delay that captures both preemptive and non-preemptive transition scenarios, replacing the conservative simulation-based estimates used in prior work. We derive sufficient schedulability conditions that account for mode-dependent execution budgets and inter-mode jitters, and prove that these conditions are necessary for a broader class of task models. Additionally, we present a priority assignment algorithm that jointly optimizes for schedulability and control performance. Evaluation on synthetic task sets and an automotive case study drawn from powertrain control applications demonstrates that MARTA reduces analytical pessimism by up to 34% compared to state-of-the-art multi-mode analysis while maintaining tight theoretical bounds, enabling more efficient utilization of real-time embedded platforms.

We introduce BlockCPS, a novel decentralized security architecture for cyber-physical systems that fundamentally reimagines intrusion detection by replacing traditional centralized security mechanisms with a permissioned blockchain-based detection framework. Prior approaches to CPS security rely on centralized anomaly detection nodes, creating single points of failure and limiting scalability in large-scale deployments such as smart grids and automotive networks. BlockCPS proposes that distributed consensus among CPS nodes can serve as both the detection mechanism and the decision-making authority for security responses, establishing a new architectural paradigm. The system implements a lightweight reputation-based Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocol specifically optimized for resource-constrained embedded devices, achieving agreement among sensor network nodes without the computational overhead of classical BFT. Each node maintains a local intrusion detection model, and detection results are propagated through the blockchain as verifiable transactions, enabling collective intelligence to override compromised or erroneous local judgments. We instantiate BlockCPS in a smart grid protection scenario involving power substation automation, demonstrating that the architecture detects and isolates false data injection attacks within sub-second latency while tolerating up to one-third malicious nodes. A full-scale co-simulation with power system models confirms the framework's effectiveness in maintaining grid stability under adversarial conditions.

Autonomous vehicles demand robust real-time sensor fusion under strict computational budgets, yet existing fusion architectures struggle to adapt dynamically to environmental conditions and sensor degradation. We present AdaptFuse, an adaptive sensor fusion architecture for automotive cyber-physical systems that significantly extends traditional Extended Kalman Filter-based approaches through context-aware reconfiguration. While prior work on sensor networks for autonomous driving has focused on single-shot fusion accuracy, AdaptFuse addresses the challenge of maintaining perception reliability across diverse operating conditions including adverse weather, sensor noise variations, and partial failures. The architecture introduces a run-time monitoring module that assesses the health and informativeness of each sensor stream using information-theoretic metrics, and a dynamic weighting engine that reallocates fusion emphasis without interrupting real-time operation. The system implements a hierarchical sensor fusion pipeline—raw measurements first undergo pre-processing and anomaly detection, then enter a bank of parallel filter instances tailored to specific scenarios, with a meta-scheduler selecting the appropriate instance based on environmental context. We validate AdaptFuse through hardware-in-the-loop simulation using camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs, demonstrating a 41% reduction in state estimation error during degraded sensor conditions and graceful degradation behavior that maintains safe operation for an additional 2.3 seconds following complete camera failure. The design is implemented on an automotive-grade embedded platform meeting ISO 26262 timing requirements.
